pitch.heading: Why Blueprint Modular
pitch.item1: Reusable components ? Text, data, charts, forms, layout. All in the docs.
pitch.item2: Python only ? No front-end to wire. You declare, the UI updates.
pitch.item3: Docs and deployment included ? Installation, API, VPS/Docker deployment step by step.

diff.heading: What BPM offers that others don't
diff.intro: Granular reactivity, design system, registry and config-driven layout: four strengths no other Python data framework offers natively.
diff.item1: Granular reactivity + simple syntax ? Targeted component updates (refs, reactive store) without full script re-run.
diff.item2: Consistent design system (bpm.*) ? Centralised tokens; customisation via CSS variables.
diff.item3: Registry $ and @ ? Reactive refs for state; decorators for pages, sidebar, cache.
diff.item4: Config-driven layout ? One app.config.js for everything; duplicate an app = edit that file.

faq.metaDesc: Frequently asked questions about Blueprint Modular.
faq.lead: Frequently asked questions about Blueprint Modular.
faq.a1: No. BPM is an alternative to Streamlit: same idea (Python only, no HTML/JS), but a different architecture and APIs (refs, design system, config-driven layout). You cannot mix Streamlit and BPM code in the same app.
faq.q2: Can I use BPM with a SQL database?
faq.a2: Yes. Connect to your database from Python (sqlite3, psycopg2, etc.) and pass the results to bpm.table, bpm.dataframe or charts. To avoid reopening the connection on each rerun, use bpm.connection() or @bpm.cache_resource (when available).
faq.a3: BPM does not provide a built-in login component. You can: (1) put a reverse proxy (Nginx) that handles auth upstream; (2) check a token/session in app.py (cookie, header) and show a login page with BPM inputs; (3) use an external service (OAuth, Auth0). Templates (e.g. a login page) will be documented in the Components section.
faq.a4: Not natively. BPM is designed for apps served by bpm run app.py (request → script execution → HTML render cycle). In a Jupyter notebook the execution model is different (cells, kernel). For quick prototyping in a notebook, use the usual libraries (pandas, matplotlib, ipywidgets).
faq.q5: What is the difference between bpm.table and bpm.dataframe?
faq.a5: bpm.table displays a simple table (list of lists or DataFrame) styled consistently with the design system. bpm.dataframe is intended for pandas DataFrames with sorting, pagination and column formatting. Both register a render node; the current implementation may not yet distinguish the two on the frontend — see API Reference — Data.
faq.q6: How do I customise the colours?
faq.a6: Via bpm.theme(primary_color="#d4af37") (or equivalent) or by overriding the CSS variables in your theme sheet (theme.css or doc.css). The tokens (primary colour, background, border) are documented in Config.
faq.a7: Yes. The code is in the project repository (see the Roadmap for the link once the repo is public).
faq.q8: Where do I report a bug?
faq.a8: Once the repository is public, use GitHub issues to report a bug (describing the problem, the Python version and the steps to reproduce). In the meantime, see the Roadmap.

troubleshooting.metaDesc: Common troubleshooting for BPM apps: problem, cause, solution.
troubleshooting.lead: Problem → cause → solution. Common troubleshooting for BPM apps.
troubleshooting.p1cause: Cause — The bpm console script is not in the PATH (venv not activated or pip install without -e .).
troubleshooting.p1sol: Solution — Activate the virtual environment: source .venv/bin/activate (Linux/macOS) or .venv\Scripts\activate (Windows). Or run it explicitly: python -m bpm.cli run app.py.
troubleshooting.p2h: 2. Port already in use at startup
troubleshooting.p2cause: Cause — Another process is using the default port (8501).
troubleshooting.p2sol: Solution — Change the port: bpm run app.py --port 8502 or python -m bpm.cli run app.py --port 8502.
troubleshooting.p3h: 3. The app fully reloads on every click
troubleshooting.p3cause: Cause — Current behaviour: each interaction triggers a full script re-run (like Streamlit).
troubleshooting.p3sol: Solution — This is expected for now. Granular reactivity (targeted update without a re-run) is planned (WebSocket/SSE) — see the Roadmap.
troubleshooting.p4cause: Cause — Refs (bpm.ref) and targeted updates are not yet implemented on the Python server / protocol side.
troubleshooting.p4sol: Solution — Use bpm.session_state to persist state between runs. Refs will be documented once support is in place.
troubleshooting.p5cause: Cause — Nginx cannot reach the BPM server (process stopped, wrong port, or BPM listening on 127.0.0.1 only).
troubleshooting.p5sol: Solution — Check that the BPM service is running: systemctl status blueprint-modular. Check that proxy_pass points to the right port (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8501). Check the Nginx logs and the service's systemd journal.
troubleshooting.p6cause: Cause — Expired Let's Encrypt certificate or Certbot renewal not configured.
troubleshooting.p6sol: Solution — Renew: certbot renew. Check the cron job or systemd timer for automatic renewal. Check that the browser trusts the certificate (no self-signed in prod without import).
troubleshooting.p7cause: Cause — Python runs in an environment where the BPM package is not installed (another venv, another interpreter).
troubleshooting.p7sol: Solution — Install the package: pip install blueprint-modular (PyPI). If you contribute to the repo: pip install -e . from the repo root (Blueprint-Modular/blueprint-modular). Check with python -c "import bpm; print(bpm.__file__)".
troubleshooting.helpCta: A question? See the FAQ and the Roadmap.

reference.metaDesc: API reference for Blueprint Modular (BPM) components. Signature, parameters and examples.
reference.metricLead: Displays an indicator with a label, a value and an optional delta (positive/negative change).
reference.metricLabelDesc: Title or header of the metric.
reference.metricValueDesc: Displayed value. null or undefined is rendered as an em dash.
reference.metricDeltaDesc: Change shown with an arrow (↑ if positive, ↓ if negative). Colour based on deltaType. If null, no arrow.
reference.metricDeltaTypeDesc: "normal": positive = green, negative = red. "inverse": positive = red, negative = green (e.g. costs).
reference.metricDeltaDecimalsDesc: Number of decimals for the delta display.
reference.metricCurrencyDesc: Symbol for the delta (EUR, USD, GBP, JPY, CHF, CAD, AUD). Empty string for a percentage.
reference.metricHelpDesc: Tooltip shown next to the label (? icon).
reference.metricEx2: Example 2: Several metrics side by side
reference.metricEx3Note: For an indicator where a decrease is positive (e.g. cost), use deltaType="inverse".
reference.buttonLead: Button with variants (primary, secondary, danger) and sizes (small, medium, large).
reference.buttonFullWidthDesc: The button takes the full available width.
reference.selectLead: Dropdown list with options, label, help and placeholder. Handles outside click and Escape.
reference.selectOnChangeDesc: Called with the new value on change.
reference.selectPlaceholderDesc: Text shown when no value is selected.
reference.tableLead: Sortable table. Columns with key, label, optionally align. Data = array of objects.
reference.tableColumnsDesc: { key, label, align? }. key used for sorting if present.
reference.tableDataDesc: Rows (objects). Keys must match the columns' key.
reference.tableOnRowClickDesc: Called with the row on click.
reference.numberLead: Numeric field with label, min/max/step, help. Controlled or uncontrolled.
reference.numberOnChangeDesc: Called with the new value (number or string in controlled mode).
reference.dateLead: Date picker (type date) with label, min/max and help.
reference.colorLead: Colour picker (input color) with label and hex value.
reference.colorOnChangeDesc: Called with the new hex value.
reference.tabsLead: Tabs with content. tabs = array of { label, content } or strings.
reference.tabsDefaultDesc: Index of the active tab on mount.
reference.tabsOnChangeDesc: Called with the index on tab change.
reference.messageLead: Message block with type info, success, warning or error.
reference.modalLead: Modal window with title, Escape close and backdrop click. Rendered in a portal.
reference.toastLead: Toast notifications. Wrap the app with ToastProvider and use the useToast() hook.
reference.spinnerLead: Loading indicator with optional text and small, medium, large sizes.
reference.tooltipLead: Tooltip (MUI). text = content, position = top, bottom, left, right, top-start, etc.
reference.titleLead: Title with levels 1–4. Level 1 shows the logo (optional onLogoClick). Exports Title1, Title2, Title3, Title4.
reference.panelLead: Informational panel (alerts, states). Variants: info, warning, error, success.
reference.boxLead: Block with title, status, details. Optional isConnected for green/red styling.
reference.expanderLead: Collapsible block with title. defaultExpanded to open by default.

concepts.metaDesc: How BPM serves your app and which deployment options to choose: VPS + Nginx, Docker, typical architecture.
concepts.lead: How BPM serves your app and which deployment options to choose.
concepts.pServe: bpm run app.py starts a local HTTP server. In production, this server runs in the background (systemd or Docker).
concepts.cardDockerDesc: Isolation and portability. Ideal for teams.
concepts.pArch: In production, a BPM app relies on:
concepts.liPython: Python process — runs your script (bpm run app.py via systemd or Docker).
concepts.liHttp: HTTP server — BPM serves the UI (HTML/JS) and handles requests (clicks, re-run).
concepts.liProxy: Reverse proxy — Nginx (or another) for SSL, domain, load balancing.
concepts.liDomain: Domain pointing to the VPS (for SSL)

platforms.metaDesc: Deployment guides for a BPM app: VPS Ubuntu + Nginx + systemd (main) and Docker.
platforms.lead: Deployment guides: VPS Ubuntu + Nginx + systemd (main), Docker.
platforms.cardDockerDesc: Isolation and portability. Ideal for teams.
platforms.pVps: Recommended for hosting a BPM app on a dedicated server.
platforms.h3Step1: Step 1  —  Install BPM on the server
platforms.pStep1: The repository is open source (Blueprint-Modular/blueprint-modular). Use pip install blueprint-modular (PyPI) to install BPM on the server. To contribute: clone the repository then pip install -e ..
platforms.pStep1b: Then create an app.py (or use bpm init) in a deployment directory, e.g. /var/www/blueprint-modular, and point WorkingDirectory to that folder (see Step 2).
platforms.pStep2b: Then: systemctl daemon-reload, systemctl enable blueprint-modular, systemctl start blueprint-modular.
platforms.pStep3: Nginx vhost that proxies to http://127.0.0.1:8501. See deploy/nginx.conf or examples in the repo.
platforms.pStep5: With PyPI: source .venv/bin/activate && pip install --upgrade blueprint-modular && systemctl restart blueprint-modular. If you deploy from the repository (access required): git pull then restart, or deploy/deploy-from-git.sh.
platforms.pDockerCompose: docker-compose.yml with Nginx (optional): reverse proxy + SSL. See examples in the repo.
platforms.pDockerCloud: <small>There is no "BPM Cloud" platform for now.</small>
platforms.helpCta: A question? Check the FAQ and What's left to do.

fundamentals.metaDesc: The BPM mental model, the render cycle, reactive refs and the design system.
fundamentals.lead: The BPM mental model, the render cycle, refs and the design system.
fundamentals.pMental: BPM works like a declaration: you describe what you want to display, BPM handles the rendering. No HTML, no manual callbacks.
fundamentals.liLaunch: At launch — bpm run executes app.py from top to bottom. Each call (bpm.title, bpm.button, etc.) registers a render node.
fundamentals.liInteraction: On each interaction — Click on a button → HTTP request with ?clicked= → update of bpm.session_state → script re-run. Only the components concerned can be refreshed (granular reactivity planned; today a full re-run like Streamlit).
fundamentals.liDiff: Difference from Streamlit — BPM ultimately aims for targeted updates without re-executing the whole script (reactive refs, frontend store).
fundamentals.previewCycle: [ Cycle diagram: launch → script execution → nodes → HTML ; click → request → session_state → re-run ]
fundamentals.pRefs: Refs let you keep reactive state: only the part of the interface that reads the ref updates.
fundamentals.noteRefs: Note — Today, each click triggers a full script re-run (like Streamlit). A WebSocket or SSE mode is planned to update only the components concerned, without a full reload.
fundamentals.pDecorators: BPM provides decorators to structure the app: pages, sidebar, cache.
fundamentals.pDecoratorsEnd: These APIs are being aligned between the Python runtime and the frontend.
fundamentals.pConfig: For apps that use the BPM React frontend, configuration is done via app.config.js. The 4 main keys: title, theme, sidebar, pages. See Config.
fundamentals.pDesign: All components share the same CSS tokens (primary color, spacing, typography). Customize via bpm.theme(primary_color="#d4af37") or by overriding the variables in theme.css (or doc.css).

installation.lead: Installation of the Python package and the BPM runtime (bpm run). For the demo app (Next.js), see Deploy.
installation.h2All: Everything that needs to be installed
installation.liRuntime: Python runtime (bpm run): Python 3.9+, pip, then pip install blueprint-modular.
installation.liApp: Dashboard application (Next.js, Wiki, AI, Documents, Asset Management modules, etc.): Node.js, npm, PostgreSQL, Prisma (via npm install and npx prisma migrate deploy). See docs/DATABASE.md and Deploy.
installation.liAiLocal: Local AI in the Python runtime (bpm.ask, bpm.chat, etc.): bpm setup installs Ollama and the default model. See AI models Getting-started workflow.
installation.pWorkflow: To create and run a BPM app with local AI in a few commands:
installation.pWorkflowEnd: bpm setup installs Ollama if needed, starts the service and downloads the default model (e.g. llama3.2). Then you can use bpm.ask(), bpm.chat(), bpm.summarize() and bpm.analyze() in your app.py.
installation.pModels: For the AI module, document analysis and the “By AI” sandbox, the application uses Ollama locally by default. You need to install Ollama then download at least one model.
installation.olInstall: Install Ollama: ollama.com (Linux, macOS, Windows).
installation.olService: Start the Ollama service (often automatic after installation).
installation.olPullIntro: Download a recommended model (just one is enough to start):
installation.olPullMore: Other possible models: ollama pull qwen2.5:7b, ollama pull mistral:7b-instruct, ollama pull llama3.2:3b.
installation.olConfig: Configure the app: in .env.local, set AI_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:11434 (or your Ollama server URL) and optionally AI_MODEL=qwen3:8b. In development without Ollama: AI_MOCK=true.

integration.metaDesc: Reference for integrating all BPM modules and components into another application (copy/sync, API, PyPI).
integration.lead: This page is the public reference for integrating Blueprint Modular's business modules and BPM components into another application, without access to the Git repository.
integration.h2Use: What to do to use the modules
integration.pUse: As a developer or user, here are the steps to integrate Blueprint Modular modules into your own application:
integration.stepDownload: Download the bundle — Get the official archive: blueprint-modules-latest.zip (or a pinned version blueprint-modules-vX.Y.Z.zip from versions.html). No account or Git access required.
integration.stepUnzip: Unzip — Open the zip in a temporary directory. You get the folders modules/, components/bpm/, lib/, prisma/ and the README-BUNDLE.md.
integration.stepCopy:
Copy into your project — Paste the folders into your Next.js application (or equivalent):
  • modules/* → e.g. app/(app)/modules/blueprint/ (or your route structure)
  • components/bpm/ → components/bpm/
  • lib/* → lib/ (merging with your existing files if needed)
  • Excerpts from prisma/schema.prisma → merge the models into your schema.prisma (see API and DB docs).
integration.stepEnv: Configure the environment — Set at minimum DATABASE_URL, NEXTAUTH_SECRET, NEXTAUTH_URL. Depending on the modules: domain config (Asset Management), AI_SERVER_URL (AI module), etc. See each module’s docs and .env.example in the source repository.
integration.stepDb: Database — Run npx prisma generate, then npx prisma migrate deploy (or merge the migrations according to your strategy). The tables used by each module are described in the deployed documentation (DATABASE.md in the repository).
integration.stepStyles: Styles — Copy the useful parts of app/globals.css (--bpm-* variables, .bpm-* classes, optionally .asset-manager-page if you use Asset Management).
integration.stepNav: Navigation — Adapt your menu or layout to point to the routes of the copied modules (e.g. /modules/asset-manager/..., /modules/wiki).
integration.pUseEnd: For a detailed list of modules and API routes, see the All modules (UI) and API (backend routes) sections below.
integration.pIp: Blueprint Modular (module code, BPM components, libraries delivered in the bundle or the PyPI package) is distributed under the MIT license. By using the modules you accept the terms of this license.
integration.ipCan: What you can do: use, modify, merge, publish and distribute the Blueprint Modular code in your own projects (including commercial ones). You remain the owner of the code you write; integrating our modules into your application does not transfer ownership of your code to Blueprint Modular.
integration.ipMust: What you must do: keep the license notice and the Blueprint Modular copyright on the files you reuse as-is (or on derived parts, per the MIT). A mention in your documentation or a NOTICE file is recommended (e.g. “This project includes Blueprint Modular modules, MIT license”).
integration.ipNoWarranty: No warranty: the software is provided “as is”, without warranty of any kind. Use at your own risk.
integration.pIpEnd: For the full text of the MIT license, see the LICENSE file at the root of the source repository or the PyPI package. If in doubt about commercial use or intellectual property, contact the project maintainer (see the docs or the repository).
integration.h2NoGit: Without Git access: download the bundle
integration.pNoGit: Any developer can get the modules and components without access to the repository by downloading the official zip:
integration.noGitSpecific: Specific version: ../downloads/blueprint-modules-vX.Y.Z.zip (see versions.html for the current version)
integration.pNoGitZip: The zip contains: modules/ (all UI modules), components/bpm/ (design system), lib/, prisma/ (schema and migrations), and a README-BUNDLE.md with instructions for copying into your project. No Git clone needed.
integration.pNoGitSync: In your sync script (or manually): download the zip from the URL above, unzip, then copy the folders into your application as described in the bundle README.
integration.pPypi: If you have installed pip install blueprint-modular, a reference file is included in the package. In Python:
integration.pPypiEnd: The manifest.json contains the URL of this page and the list of modules/components. See also Versions.
integration.pModules: Each module is a section under app/(app)/modules// in the source repository. List of available modules:
integration.modAssetManager: Asset Management: dashboard, assets, tickets, MAD, contracts, knowledge, changes, CMDB, audit.
integration.pApi: The API routes are exposed under app/api/. Main prefixes:
integration.apiWiki: Articles, revisions, comments, backlinks, export, semantic-search, tags.
integration.apiAssetManager: Config, domains, assets, tickets, assignments, contracts, knowledge, changes, ci-relations, movements, audit-log, etc.

integration.pCopySync: To integrate the modules and components into another application without access to the repository, you can:
integration.copyApi: Call the API of a deployed Blueprint Modular instance (see Deploy). Your app sends HTTP requests to the routes listed above.
integration.copyCode: Get the code if you have access to the repository (clone, submodule): copy app/(app)/modules/, app/api/, components/bpm/, lib/ (as needed), prisma/schema.prisma and migrations, and the BPM-related parts of app/globals.css. Full details in the INTEGRATION.md file at the root of the repository (visible only with repo access).

whyBpm.metaDesc: Why Blueprint Modular is the best solution: granular reactivity, design system, $ and @ registry, config-driven layout.
whyBpm.lead: Blueprint Modular combines a simple syntax (all in Python, no frontend to wire up) with advantages that other frameworks don't offer natively.
whyBpm.p1One: Traditional frameworks force a choice between simplicity (the whole script re-runs on every click) and targeted reactivity (explicit callbacks everywhere). BPM aims for both: a syntax as simple as possible, with reactive refs (bpm.ref("x")) so that only the components concerned update — no full page re-run.
whyBpm.p2One: On the frontend, a reactive store and a useReactive(key) hook already enable reactive interfaces without reloading everything.
whyBpm.pTwo: All BPM components share the same tokens (colors, spacing, typography) via theme.css. You customize the app by overriding CSS variables, without touching component code. No other Python framework for data offers a real native design system.
whyBpm.p3Intro: BPM introduces a registry with two key ideas:
whyBpm.liDollar: $ — Reactive refs: named state (bpm.ref("compteur")) with .get(), .set(), .subscribe(). Only the widgets that read this ref refresh.
whyBpm.liAt: @ — Block registration: @bpm.page("rapports"), @bpm.sidebar, @bpm.cache_data. The layout can render “the block registered under this name”.
whyBpm.p3End: No competitor offers this dual semantics natively.
whyBpm.pFour: Sidebar, header, pages and links are described in a single config file. Duplicating an app = copy the project and edit this file. No need to touch the page code or the Layout. No other framework lets you clone an app by changing just one file.
whyBpm.liComponents: Components — Text, data, charts, inputs, layout, feedback (Message, Modal, Toast, Spinner, Progress, Skeleton, EmptyState…), structure (Card, Accordion, Stepper, Drawer, FAB, Grid, TopNav, TreeView, Timeline, Breadcrumb, Chip, Avatar…). All with a className prop for your styles.
whyBpm.liDoc: Documentation — Installation, fundamentals, first app, API reference, VPS/Docker deployment, FAQ, cheat sheet.
whyBpm.liDeploy: Deployment — Guides for VPS (Nginx, systemd), Docker, and deployment scripts from Git.
whyBpm.pSummary: BPM is the solution that gives you: Python only, simple syntax, targeted reactivity, consistent design system, registry for state and blocks, and config-driven layout to duplicate an app in one file. All documented and deployable without lock-in.
whyBpm.pNext: Next: Installation — Install BPM and run your first command.

modulesIndex.metaDesc: BPM add-ins: ready-made modules (Wiki, AI, Monitoring, IBKR, Document analysis) to call simply with bpm.use_module().
modulesIndex.lead: Add-ins are ready-made modules: ready-to-use pages or blocks that you can call simply in your BPM apps, without rewriting everything. Unlike components (UI building blocks), an add-in is a complete functional page.
modulesIndex.s1p: An add-in (module) is a page or block provided by BPM or by the community: Wiki, AI, Monitoring, IBKR, Document analysis, etc. You integrate it in a few lines instead of recoding the logic and the UI.
modulesIndex.s1li1: Simple call: once the module is available, you add it to your app with a dedicated API (see below).
modulesIndex.s1li2: Reusable: the same module usable across several apps, with or without customization.
modulesIndex.s1li3: Composable: you can combine several add-ins (e.g. Wiki + AI) in a single app.
modulesIndex.s2h2: How to call a module (simple call)
modulesIndex.s2p1: When an add-in is available, you integrate it in one or a few lines. Example of intended usage:
modulesIndex.s2p2: The sidebar and navigation are then updated automatically to display the pages of the added modules. The modules listed below are either already available (you can call them this way) or planned in the roadmap — in which case the detail page indicates "planned" and the link to What's left to do.
